claim: Propagation of slow intrinsic brain activity has been widely observed in electrophysiological studies of slow wave sleep (SWS).
source: Propagation of slow intrinsic brain activity has been widely observed in electrophysiogical studies of slow wave sleep (SWS).
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior electrophysiological studies of SWS, as indicated by the context of the abstract.

claim: In human resting state fMRI (rs-fMRI), intrinsic activity has been understood predominantly in terms of zero-lag temporal synchrony (functional connectivity) within systems known as resting state networks (RSNs).
source: However, in human resting state fMRI (rs-fMRI), intrinsic activity has been understood predominantly in terms of zero-lag temporal synchrony (functional connectivity) within systems known as resting state networks (RSNs).
evidence: This claim reflects established understanding in the field of rs-fMRI research.

claim: Prior rs-fMRI studies have found that RSNs are generally preserved across wake and sleep.
source: Prior rs-fMRI studies have found that RSNs are generally preserved across wake and sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research in the field.

claim: Ordered propagation is preserved within traditionally defined RSNs but lost between RSNs during SWS.
source: Broadly, ordered propagation is preserved within traditionally defined RSNs but lost between RSNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 5.

claim: Propagation between cerebral cortex and subcortical structures reverses directions during SWS compared to wake.
source: Additionally, propagation between cerebral cortex and subcortical structures reverses directions, and intra-cortical propagation becomes reorganized, especially in visual and sensorimotor cortices.
evidence: This claim is supported by the seed-based lag maps shown in Figure 3.

claim: Intra-cortical propagation becomes reorganized during SWS, especially in visual and sensorimotor cortices.
source: Additionally, propagation between cerebral cortex and subcortical structures reverses directions, and intra-cortical propagation becomes reorganized, especially in visual and sensorimotor cortices.
evidence: This claim is supported by the lag maps shown in Figures 2, 4, and 5.

claim: Sleep is a state during which interactions with the environment are greatly attenuated.
source: Sleep is a state during which interactions with the environment are greatly attenuated.
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of sleep based on general scientific knowledge.

claim: Nearly all animals sleep, suggesting that sleep is essential to normal physiology.
source: Nevertheless, nearly all animals sleep, suggesting that sleep is essential to normal physiology (Cirelli and Tononi, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cirelli and Tononi, 2008.

claim: In most mammals, including humans, prolonged sleep deprivation leads to impaired performance, psychosis, and eventually death.
source: In most mammals, including humans, prolonged sleep deprivation leads to impaired performance, psychosis, and eventually death (Brown et al., 2012; Everson et al., 1989; Rechtschaffen, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Sleep is attended by changes in gene expression.
source: Sleep is attended by changes in gene expression (Abel et al., 2013; Cirelli and Tononi, 2000), neuromodulator levels (Brown et al., 2012), metabolism (Boyle et al., 1994; Braun et al., 1997), and markedly altered patterns of neural activity (Dang-Vu, 2012; Loomis et al., 1935; McCormick and Bal, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Abel et al., 2013 and Cirelli and Tononi, 2000.

claim: Sleep is attended by changes in neuromodulator levels.
source: Sleep is attended by changes in gene expression (Abel et al., 2013; Cirelli and Tononi, 2000), neuromodulator levels (Brown et al., 2012), metabolism (Boyle et al., 1994; Braun et al., 1997), and markedly altered patterns of neural activity (Dang-Vu, 2012; Loomis et al., 1935; McCormick and Bal, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brown et al., 2012.

claim: Sleep is attended by changes in metabolism.
source: Sleep is attended by changes in gene expression (Abel et al., 2013; Cirelli and Tononi, 2000), neuromodulator levels (Brown et al., 2012), metabolism (Boyle et al., 1994; Braun et al., 1997), and markedly altered patterns of neural activity (Dang-Vu, 2012; Loomis et al., 1935; McCormick and Bal, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boyle et al., 1994 and Braun et al., 1997.

claim: Sleep is attended by markedly altered patterns of neural activity.
source: Sleep is attended by changes in gene expression (Abel et al., 2013; Cirelli and Tononi, 2000), neuromodulator levels (Brown et al., 2012), metabolism (Boyle et al., 1994; Braun et al., 1997), and markedly altered patterns of neural activity (Dang-Vu, 2012; Loomis et al., 1935; McCormick and Bal, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dang-Vu, 2012; Loomis et al., 1935; and McCormick and Bal, 1997.

claim: The fundamental functions of sleep remain elusive.
source: Yet, the fundamental functions of sleep remain elusive.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Slow wave sleep (SWS) is the deepest stage of sleep.
source: Sleep conventionally is divided into stages, the deepest of which is slow wave sleep (SWS; also known as N3 sleep) (Soeffing et al., 2008; Rechtschaffen and Kales, 1968).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Soeffing et al., 2008 and Rechtschaffen and Kales, 1968.

claim: The electrophysiologic hallmark of SWS is the slow oscillation, which manifests as periodic alternations of membrane potential (Up/Down states) at frequencies in the range of 0.5–1.5 Hz.
source: The electrophysiologic hallmark of SWS is the slow oscillation, which manifests as periodic alternations of membrane potential, also known as Up/Down states (UDSs), characteristically at frequencies in the range of 0.5–1.5 Hz (Achermann and Borbély, 1997; Steriade et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Achermann and Borbély, 1997 and Steriade et al., 1993.

claim: Slow oscillations are locally synchronous but exhibit apparent propagation over the whole brain on a time scale of 100's of milliseconds.
source: As observed with extracellular local field potential (LFP) recordings, slow oscillations are locally synchronous but exhibit apparent propagation over the whole brain on a time scale of 100's of milliseconds (Hahn et al., 2012; Nir et al., 2011; Riedner et al., 2007; Sheroziya and Timofeev, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hahn et al., 2012; Nir et al., 2011; Riedner et al., 2007; and Sheroziya and Timofeev, 2014.

claim: Similar patterns of propagation have been observed using electroencephalography (EEG), in which SWS manifests as a predominance of high amplitude, 1–4 Hz (delta) rhythms.
source: Similar patterns of propagation have also been observed using electroencephalography (EEG), in which SWS manifests as a predominance of high amplitude, 1–4 Hz (delta) rhythms (Massimini et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Massimini et al., 2004.

claim: Infra-slow (<0.1 Hz) intrinsic activity recorded using rs-fMRI has been understood predominantly in terms of zero-lag temporal synchrony (functional connectivity) within resting state networks (RSNs).
source: Infra-slow (<0.1 Hz) intrinsic (equivalently, spontaneous) activity recorded using rs-fMRI has been understood predominantly in terms of zero-lag temporal synchrony (functional connectivity) within systems known as resting state networks (RSNs) (Beckmann et al., 2005; Biswal et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Beckmann et al., 2005 and Biswal et al., 2010.

claim: Prior rs-fMRI studies have found that RSNs are generally preserved across wake and SWS.
source: Prior rs-fMRI studies have found that RSNs are generally preserved across wake and SWS (Horovitz et al., 2009; Larson-Prior et al., 2009; Picchioni et al., 2013; Sämann et al., 2011; Tagliazucchi et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Conventional functional connectivity analyses assume temporal synchronicity and make no provision for the possibility that intrinsic activity may propagate between regions.
source: Importantly, conventional functional connectivity analyses assume temporal synchronicity and make no provision for the possibility that intrinsic activity may propagate between regions.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of conventional analytical methods.

claim: The BOLD signal exhibits highly reproducible temporal lag patterns on a time scale of ~1 s in awake, normal humans.
source: Using this technique, we previously demonstrated, in awake, normal humans, that the blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) signal exhibits highly reproducible temporal lag patterns on a time scale of ~1 s; some regions are systematically early with respect to the rest of brain, whereas other regions are systematically late (Mitra et al., 2014; 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mitra et al., 2014 and 2015.

claim: Temporal lags in BOLD signal activity are altered, with appropriate focality, by prior performance of motor tasks as well as by time of day.
source: Moreover, temporal lags in BOLD signal activity are altered, with appropriate focality, by prior performance of motor tasks as well as by time of day (Mitra et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mitra et al., 2014.

claim: The temporal scale of BOLD signal propagation is much slower than axonal transmission via fiber tracts.
source: In particular, the temporal scale of this phenomenology is much slower than axonal transmission via fiber tracts (Caminiti et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Caminiti et al., 2009.

claim: SWS is believed to represent an off-line state during which propagated slow activity plays a central role in the consolidation of memory.
source: First, SWS is believed to represent an off-line state during which propagated slow activity plays a central role in the consolidation of memory (Born et al., 2006; Maquet, 2001; Marshall et al., 2006; Stickgold, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Born et al., 2006; Maquet, 2001; Marshall et al., 2006; and Stickgold, 2005.

claim: Propagation along the anterior-posterior axis of the brain has been linked to consolidation of declarative memory.
source: In particular, propagation along the anterior-posterior axis of the brain has been linked to consolidation of declarative memory (Marshall et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Marshall et al., 2006.

claim: Loss of environmental awareness during SWS is thought to be mediated by thalamic hyperpolarization, which is modulated by propagation of slow (<1 Hz) activity from cortex to thalamus.
source: Second, loss of environmental awareness during SWS is thought to be mediated by thalamic hyperpolarization, which is modulated by propagation of slow (<1 Hz) activity from cortex to thalamus (Blethyn et al., 2006; Hughes et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Blethyn et al., 2006 and Hughes et al., 2002.

claim: Evidence of propagation from cortex to thalamus has never been observed in vivo.
source: Evidence of such propagation has never been observed in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of prior evidence.

claim: It has been theorized that reduced subjective awareness ('unconsciousness') during SWS results from loss of integration across networks.
source: Finally, it has been theorized that reduced subjective awareness ('unconsciousness') during SWS results from loss of integration across networks (Mashour, 2005; Tononi, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mashour, 2005 and Tononi, 2004.

claim: Thalamus is early (blue) during wake but late (red) during SWS.
source: For example, thalamus is early (blue) during wake but late (red) during SWS; the opposite shift is evident in visual cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the lag projection maps shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Visual cortex exhibits an opposite shift to thalamus, being late during wake and early during SWS.
source: For example, thalamus is early (blue) during wake but late (red) during SWS; the opposite shift is evident in visual cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the lag projection maps shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Statistically significant clusters in the wake vs. SWS comparison are centered on putamen bilaterally, thalamus, paracentral lobule (PCL), visual cortex, medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), and brainstem.
source: These clusters are centered on putamen bilaterally, thalamus, paracentral lobule (PCL), visual cortex, medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), and brainstem.
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 2C showing statistically significant clusters.

claim: During wake, the cerebral cortex is generally late with respect to subcortical regions.
source: During wake, the cerebral cortex is generally late (yellow/red hues) with respect to subcortical regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the seed-based lag maps shown in Figure 3.

claim: The cerebral cortex becomes early with respect to subcortical areas during SWS.
source: The cerebral cortex becomes early (blue/green hues) with respect to subcortical areas during SWS.
evidence: This claim is supported by the seed-based lag maps shown in Figure 3.

claim: All significant lag differences between wake and SWS are negative (blue), and predominantly found in cortex.
source: All significant lag differences are negative (blue), and predominantly found in cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the lag difference maps shown in Figure 3.

claim: Pre-frontal cortex becomes markedly early with respect to the posterior parts of the brain during SWS.
source: Pre-frontal cortex becomes markedly early with respect to the posterior parts of the brain (pink arrows in A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the seed-based lag maps shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: A 'front-to-back' propagation pattern suggests slow wave propagation in SWS.
source: This feature suggests a 'front-to-back' propagation of slow waves in SWS (Massimini et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the data and a citation to Massimini et al., 2004.

claim: Lag structure in the brainstem and thalamus is relatively constant across wake and SWS.
source: Lag structure in the brainstem and thalamus is relatively constant (pink ovals in A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the seed-based lag maps shown in Figure 3A and 3C.

claim: Nearly the entire cortex is late with respect to visual cortex during SWS.
source: Panel A shows that, whereas the visual seed is neither wholly late nor early in wake, nearly the entire cortex is late with respect to visual cortex during SWS.
evidence: This claim is supported by the seed-based lag maps shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) exhibits both early and late lag shifts between wake and SWS.
source: Panel B shows that medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) exhibits both early and late lag shifts between wake and SWS.
evidence: This claim is supported by the seed-based lag maps shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Many of the lag relations of the paracentral lobule seed are reversed during SWS relative to wake.
source: Panel C shows that many of the lag relations of the paracentral lobule seed are reversed during SWS relative to wake.
evidence: This claim is supported by the seed-based lag maps shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In wake, paracentral lobule leads lateral sensory-motor cortex and posterior insula.
source: For example, in wake, the seed-region leads lateral sensory-motor cortex and posterior insula.
evidence: This claim is supported by the seed-based lag maps shown in Figure 4C.

claim: These relations reverse in SWS and nearly the entire cerebral cortex becomes early with respect to the paracentral lobule.
source: These relations reverse in SWS and nearly the entire cerebral cortex becomes early with respect to the paracentral lobule.
evidence: This claim is supported by the seed-based lag maps shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The range of lag values in SWS is larger than in the wake data.
source: First, the range of lag values in SWS is larger than in the wake data, as if the speed of BOLD signal propagation has slowed.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of TD matrices shown in Figure 5.

claim: Standard deviation during wake was 0.42 ± 0.05 s, whereas SD during SWS was 0.65 ± 0.07 s.
source: SD during wake was 0.42 ± 0.05 s, whereas SD during SWS was 0.65 ± 0.07 s.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the TD matrices.

claim: The difference in standard deviation between wake and SWS was significant (p<0.01).
source: This effect was significant (p<0.01, by permutation resampling with 10,000 trials).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical testing.

claim: Inter-RSN lag structure is altered in SWS.
source: Second, inter-RSN lag structure is altered in SWS.
evidence: This claim is supported by the TD matrices shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Propagation within RSNs is relatively preserved during sleep, while propagation across RSNs is significantly altered.
source: Thus, Figure 5C demonstrates that, whereas propagation within RSNs is relatively preserved during sleep, propagation across RSNs is significantly altered.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The visual network assumes an 'all early' organization with respect to other cortical RSNs during SWS.
source: A third effect evident in Figure 5A, B is the appearance of an 'all early' organization in the visual network ('VIS', pink box) in SWS.
evidence: This claim is supported by the TD matrices shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Voxels in the visual network are earlier than nearly all other cortical voxels during SWS.
source: That is, in half the TD matrix, all cross-RSN voxel pairs involving the visual network exhibit negative (early; blue) lag values in SWS, indicating that voxels in the visual network are earlier than nearly all other cortical voxels.
evidence: This claim is supported by the TD matrices shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: The principle that no RSN leads or follows any other, which applies in wake, does not hold during SWS.
source: Thus, the principle, which applies in wake, that no RSN leads or follows any other (Mitra et al., 2014), does not hold during SWS.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of TD matrices and a citation to Mitra et al., 2014.

claim: During SWS, voxels in the visual network become early with respect to other cortical voxels.
source: Figure 5E shows that this principle approximately applies also in SWS except in the visual network (white asterisks). During SWS, voxels in the visual network become early with respect to other cortical voxels (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A subset of the cross-RSN sensorimotor (SMN) block assumes an 'all late' (red) configuration during SWS.
source: An analogous, but opposite feature also appears in a subset of the cross-RSN sensorimotor (SMN) block, which assumes an 'all late' (red) configuration.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The voxels that become late in SWS correspond to the paracentral lobule.
source: In other words, this set of voxels becomes late with respect to cortical BOLD signal activity in nearly all other cortical voxels during SWS. The voxels in question correspond to the paracentral lobule (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 5E and Figure 2C.

claim: Subcortical structures are early in relation to cortex during wake, but late during SWS.
source: Lag maps seeded in the thalamus, brainstem, and putamen demonstrated that subcortical structures are early in relation to cortex during wake, but late during SWS (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the seed-based lag maps shown in Figure 3.

claim: Propagation within the brainstem-thalamic axis was relatively preserved across states.
source: In contrast, propagation within the brainstem-thalamic axis was relatively preserved across states (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the seed-based lag maps shown in Figure 3.

claim: Comparison of TD matrices in wake vs. SWS revealed that inter-RSN propagation was significantly altered in SWS whereas intra-RSN propagation was relatively preserved.
source: Finally, comparison of TD matrices in wake vs. SWS revealed that inter-RSN propagation was significantly altered in SWS whereas intra-RSN propagation was relatively preserved (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The effect of SWS on zero-lag correlation structure (functional connectivity) is much more modest than the effect on lag structure.
source: By comparison, the effect of SWS on zero-lag correlation structure (functional connectivity) is much more modest (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by the functional connectivity analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: State differences in functional connectivity manifest as quantitative changes in the magnitude of correlations, for example, reduced correlations between anterior and posterior brain regions during SWS.
source: State differences in functional connectivity manifest as quantitative changes in the magnitude of correlations, for example, reduced correlations between anterior and posterior brain regions during SWS (Picchioni et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Picchioni et al., 2013.

claim: The overall topography of resting state networks (RSNs) generally is preserved across wake and SWS.
source: However, the overall topography of resting state networks (RSNs) generally is preserved (Horovitz et al., 2009; Larson-Prior et al., 2009; Picchioni et al., 2013; Sämann et al., 2011; Tagliazucchi et al., 2013) (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies and Figure 6.

claim: SWS induces focal functional connectivity changes in visual cortex, paracentral lobule, and thalamus.
source: Specifically, SWS induces focal functional connectivity changes in visual cortex, paracentral lobule, and thalamus; this topography substantially overlaps some of the presently observed lag effects (compare sagittal views in Figures 2C and 6D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of Figures 2C and 6D, E.

claim: PET studies show that SWS, as well as pathological disorders of consciousness, both are associated with prominent reductions in thalamic metabolism.
source: In a similar vein, PET studies show that SWS, as well as pathological disorders of consciousness, both are associated with prominent reductions in thalamic metabolism (Laureys, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Laureys, 2005.

claim: Several studies using invasive recordings have found that slow (0.5–4 Hz) and infra-slow (<0.1 Hz) local field potentials correspond most closely to BOLD signal fluctuations and correlation structure.
source: Several studies using invasive recordings have found that slow (0.5–4 Hz) and infra-slow (<0.1 Hz) local field potentials correspond most closely to BOLD signal fluctuations and correlation structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by the discussion of prior research.

claim: The correspondence between slow/infra-slow local field potentials and BOLD signal has been demonstrated in wake.
source: This correspondence has been demonstrated in wake (He et al., 2008; Hiltunen et al., 2014; Nir et al., 2008), sleep (He et al., 2008), and anesthesia (Pan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to He et al., 2008; Hiltunen et al., 2014; and Nir et al., 2008.

claim: The correspondence between slow/infra-slow local field potentials and BOLD signal has been demonstrated in sleep.
source: This correspondence has been demonstrated in wake (He et al., 2008; Hiltunen et al., 2014; Nir et al., 2008), sleep (He et al., 2008), and anesthesia (Pan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to He et al., 2008.

claim: The correspondence between slow/infra-slow local field potentials and BOLD signal has been demonstrated in anesthesia.
source: This correspondence has been demonstrated in wake (He et al., 2008; Hiltunen et al., 2014; Nir et al., 2008), sleep (He et al., 2008), and anesthesia (Pan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pan et al., 2013.

claim: Temporal lags in the BOLD signal may reflect propagation of slow and infra-slow electrophysiological activity.
source: Thus, a natural hypothesis is that temporal lags in the BOLD signal reflect propagation of slow and infra-slow electrophysiological activity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the correspondence between BOLD and electrophysiology.

claim: Temporal lags in infra-slow electrophysiology have not been investigated at the systems level.
source: However, as far as we are aware, temporal lags in infra-slow electrophysiology have not been investigated at the systems level.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of prior research.

claim: Propagation of slow electrophysiological activity has been widely reported.
source: On the other hand, propagation of slow activity has been widely reported.
evidence: This is a statement about the existence of prior research.

claim: UDSs classically are described as periodic at frequencies in the 0.5–1.5 Hz range, and are known to propagate on a time-scale of 100's of milliseconds.
source: UDSs classically are described as periodic at frequencies in the 0.5–1.5 Hz range, and are known to propagate on a time-scale of 100's of milliseconds (Hahn et al., 2006; McCormick et al., 2015; Petersen et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hahn et al., 2006; McCormick et al., 2015; and Petersen et al., 2003.

claim: UDSs have been described in awake, resting rodents.
source: More recently, UDSs have also been described in awake, resting rodents (Ferezou et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ferezou et al., 2007.

claim: Macro-electrode recordings show aperiodic, 1/f-like spectral content during SWS.
source: Although UDS periodicity is a characteristic of single neuron membrane potential recordings (Hahn et al., 2006; Petersen et al., 2003), macro-electrode recordings, e.g., electroencephalography (EEG) and electrocorticography (ECoG), show aperiodic, 1/f-like spectral content during SWS (He et al., 2010; Nir et al., 2011; Sirota et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to He et al., 2010; Nir et al., 2011; and Sirota et al., 2003.

claim: The spectral content of intrinsic electrophysiologic activity and rs-fMRI is 1/f-like in wake as well as SWS.
source: More generally, the spectral content of intrinsic electrophysiologic activity and rs-fMRI is 1/f-like in wake as well as SWS (He et al., 2008; Hiltunen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to He et al., 2008 and Hiltunen et al., 2014.

claim: Macro-electrode recordings of slow activity show apparent propagation on time-scales as long as 1–2 s during sleep and anesthesia.
source: Moreover, macro-electrode recordings of slow activity also show apparent propagation on time-scales as long as 1–2 s during sleep and anesthesia (Nir et al., 2011; Sirota et al., 2003), as in the present rs-fMRI data.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nir et al., 2011 and Sirota et al., 2003.

claim: Electrophysiological studies in both humans and rodents suggest that slow activity tends to originate in medial prefrontal cortex and propagate to more posterior regions.
source: Electrophysiological studies in both humans and rodents suggest that slow activity tends to originate in medial prefrontal cortex and propagate to more posterior regions (Massimini et al., 2004; Nir et al., 2011; Sheroziya and Timofeev, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Massimini et al., 2004; Nir et al., 2011; and Sheroziya and Timofeev, 2014.

claim: A 'front-to-back' propagation pattern is observed in the present study.
source: We also observe a 'front-to-back' propagation pattern (see Figures 4B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figures 4B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: A noteworthy principle that has emerged from human high-density EEG and ECoG recordings is that slow waves originate in multiple locations and propagate through multiple routes.
source: In that regard, a noteworthy principle that has emerged on the basis of human high-density EEG and ECoG recordings is that slow waves originate in multiple locations and propagate through multiple routes (Massimini et al., 2004; Murphy et al., 2009; Nir et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Massimini et al., 2004; Murphy et al., 2009; and Nir et al., 2011.

claim: A necessary algebraic consequence of slow waves originating in multiple locations is that the lag structure of propagated slow activity exists in a multi-dimensional space.
source: A necessary algebraic consequence of this principle is that the lag structure of propagated slow activity exists in a multi-dimensional space (Mitra et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mitra et al., 2015 and logical inference.

claim: The same principle of multi-dimensional lag structure applies in the current fMRI data, both during wake and SWS.
source: We confirm that the same principle applies in the current fMRI data, both during wake and SWS (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Apparent propagation of either slow or infra-slow electrophysiological activity in the awake state has not been reported in either humans or animals.
source: To the best of our knowledge, apparent propagation of either slow or infra-slow electrophysiological activity in the awake state has not been reported in either humans or animals.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of prior research.

claim: Voltage sensitive dye (VSD) studies in quietly resting rodents have demonstrated multiple patterns of propagation of slow intrinsic activity over 100's of milliseconds.
source: However, voltage sensitive dye (VSD) studies in quietly resting rodents have demonstrated multiple patterns of propagation of slow intrinsic activity over 100's of milliseconds (Mohajerani et al., 2013; Mohajerani et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mohajerani et al., 2013 and Mohajerani et al., 2010.

claim: Propagation patterns assessed using VSD are bilaterally symmetric.
source: Moreover, propagation patterns assessed using VSD are bilaterally symmetric (Mohajerani et al., 2010), as are BOLD fMRI patterns of propagation (Mitra et al., 2015; Mitra et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mohajerani et al., 2010; Mitra et al., 2015; and Mitra et al., 2014.

claim: BOLD fMRI patterns of propagation are bilaterally symmetric.
source: Moreover, propagation patterns assessed using VSD are bilaterally symmetric (Mohajerani et al., 2010), as are BOLD fMRI patterns of propagation (Mitra et al., 2015; Mitra et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mitra et al., 2015 and Mitra et al., 2014.

claim: The available evidence suggests that the BOLD signal and slow/infra-slow electrophysiological activity exhibit similarities in spectral content, correlation structure, and apparent propagation.
source: In summary, the available evidence suggests that the BOLD signal and slow/infra-slow electrophysiological activity exhibit similarities in spectral content, correlation structure, and apparent propagation.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the discussion of prior research.

claim: Slow wave sleep is believed to represent an off-line state during which slow activity enables consolidation of newly acquired memories.
source: First, slow wave sleep is believed to represent an off-line state during which slow activity enables consolidation of newly acquired memories (Born et al., 2006; Maquet, 2001; Marshall et al., 2006; Stickgold, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Born et al., 2006; Maquet, 2001; Marshall et al., 2006; and Stickgold, 2005.

claim: Human imaging studies of word-pair association tasks have shown that the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) is implicated in consolidation of declarative memory.
source: Human imaging studies of word-pair association tasks have shown that the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) is implicated in consolidation of declarative memory (Euston et al., 2012; Gais et al., 2007; Takashima et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Euston et al., 2012; Gais et al., 2007; and Takashima et al., 2006.

claim: Consolidation is accompanied by increases in mPFC activity during successful later recall.
source: Consolidation is accompanied by increases in mPFC activity during successful later recall (Gais et al., 2007; Takashima et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gais et al., 2007 and Takashima et al., 2006.

claim: Marshall and colleagues found that artificially initiating slow wave activity by applying current via frontal electrodes during SWS boosts subsequent recall.
source: Using the same task, Marshall and colleagues found that artificially initiating slow wave activity by applying current via frontal electrodes during SWS boosts subsequent recall (Marshall et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Marshall et al., 2006.

claim: The mPFC shift towards earliness during SWS may facilitate consolidation of declarative memory.
source: Thus, the available data suggest that the mPFC shift towards earliness during SWS may facilitate consolidation of declarative memory.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the integration of prior research and the present findings.

claim: SWS is thought to improve procedural memory, e.g., motor sequence learning and motor adaptation.
source: Second, SWS is also thought to improve procedural memory, e.g., motor sequence learning and motor adaptation (Stickgold, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stickgold, 2005.

claim: Putamen and paracentral lobule (PCL) are strongly associated with procedural learning.
source: We observed significant wake vs. SWS latency shifts in putamen and paracentral lobule (PCL) (Figures 2–4), both of which structures are strongly associated with procedural learning (Graybiel, 2005; Halsband and Lange, 2006; Knowlton et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Graybiel, 2005; Halsband and Lange, 2006; and Knowlton et al., 1996.

claim: The paracentral lobule is a functional component of the supplementary motor area (SMA).
source: The paracentral lobule is a functional component of the supplementary motor area (SMA) (Lim et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lim et al., 1994.

claim: Sleep-dependent improvements in procedural tasks have been postulated to involve plasticity in cortico-striatal circuits.
source: Sleep-dependent improvements in procedural tasks have been postulated to involve plasticity in cortico-striatal circuits (Doyon and Benali, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Doyon and Benali, 2005.

claim: The reversal in the temporal lag between putamen and cortex during SWS could be a correlate of off-line consolidation of procedural memory.
source: Thus, the reversal in the temporal lag between putamen and cortex (Figure 3B) during SWS could be a correlate of off-line consolidation of procedural memory.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the integration of prior research and the present findings.

claim: Altered apparent propagation in PCL may relate to offline adjustment of motor programs.
source: Similarly, altered apparent propagation in PCL may relate to offline adjustment of motor programs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the present findings.

claim: PCL lateness during SWS could represent a correlate of the abolition of motor behavior.
source: Alternatively, PCL lateness during SWS could represent a correlate of the abolition of motor behavior.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis based on the present findings.

claim: Dreaming also occurs in NREM sleep.
source: Third, we show that visual cortex is neither wholly late nor early during wake, but that nearly the entire cerebral cortex becomes late with respect to visual cortex during SWS (Figure 4A, Figure 5). This visual cortex finding may relate to the now widely recognized fact that dreaming also occurs in NREM sleep (Hobson et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hobson et al., 2000.

claim: Recent work has shown that BOLD fMRI activity in visual cortex predicts NREM dreaming.
source: Recent work has shown that BOLD fMRI activity in visual cortex predicts NREM dreaming (Horikawa et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Horikawa et al., 2013.

claim: There may exist a link between initiation of infra-slow activity in visual cortex and dreaming.
source: Hence, there may exist a link between initiation of infra-slow activity in visual cortex and dreaming.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the integration of prior research and the present findings.

claim: Wakefulness is a state during which environmental awareness is possible.
source: Wakefulness is a state during which environmental awareness is possible (Seth et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Seth et al., 2005.

claim: The thalamus plays a critical role in environmental awareness by relaying sensory signals to the cerebral cortex.
source: The thalamus plays a critical role in this state by relaying sensory signals to the cerebral cortex (Alkire et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alkire et al., 2008.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings have shown that the awake state is associated with depolarization of thalamocortical cells, which facilitates transmission of ascending input to the cortex.
source: Electrophysiological recordings have shown that the awake state is associated with depolarization of thalamocortical cells, which facilitates transmission of ascending input to the cortex (Brown et al., 2012; Franks, 2008; McCormick and Bal, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brown et al., 2012; Franks, 2008; and McCormick and Bal, 1997.

claim: During SWS, signals from the environment do not reliably reach the cortex owing to hyperpolarization of thalamocortical neurons.
source: Conversely, during SWS, signals from the environment do not reliably reach the cortex owing to hyperpolarization of thalamocortical neurons (Franks, 2008; Franks and Lieb, 1994; Hirsch et al., 1983; Steriade and Timofeev, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Franks, 2008; Franks and Lieb, 1994; Hirsch et al., 1983; and Steriade and Timofeev, 2003.

claim: The thalamus 'gates' transmission of environmental stimuli to the cortex.
source: Thus, the thalamus 'gates' transmission of environmental stimuli to the cortex.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the discussion of thalamic function.

claim: In vitro work suggests that thalamic hyperpolarization in SWS is modulated by propagation of slow (<1 Hz) activity from cortex to thalamus.
source: Moreover, in vitro work suggests that thalamic hyperpolarization in SWS is modulated by propagation of slow (<1 Hz) activity from cortex to thalamus (Blethyn et al., 2006; Hughes et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Blethyn et al., 2006 and Hughes et al., 2002.

claim: Analysis of BOLD signal fluctuations is consistent with the account that thalamic hyperpolarization in SWS is modulated by propagation of slow activity from cortex to thalamus.
source: Our analysis of BOLD signal fluctuations is consistent with this account: Cerebral cortex leads thalamus during SWS, but thalamus leads cortex during wake (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: BOLD signal propagation from brainstem to thalamus is similar in wake and SWS.
source: Importantly, BOLD signal propagation from brainstem to thalamus is similar in wake and SWS.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The thalamus is the site at which ascending signals are impeded during SWS.
source: This result suggests that the thalamus is the site at which ascending signals are impeded during SWS, in accordance with the hypothesized role of the thalamus as a sensory gate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the present findings and prior knowledge.

claim: Cross-network lag structure is extensively altered in SWS as compared to wake.
source: Figure 5 shows that cross-network lag structure is extensively altered in SWS as compared to wake.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: During wake, both diagonal- and off-diagonal blocks of the TD matrix exhibit well-ordered early, middle, and late components.
source: During wake, both diagonal- and off-diagonal blocks of the TD matrix exhibit well-ordered early, middle, and late components.
evidence: This claim is supported by the TD matrix shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cross-network and within-network propagation are comparable during wake.
source: Thus, cross-network and within-network propagation are comparable during wake.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TD matrix analysis.

claim: During SWS, apparent propagation within and across networks is no longer comparable.
source: During SWS, apparent propagation within and across networks is no longer comparable (Figure 5B,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the TD matrix analysis shown in Figure 5B and 5E.

claim: Cross-network (off-diagonal) blocks lose their 'early-to-late' structure during SWS, whereas within-network (diagonal blocks) lag structure is preserved.
source: Cross-network (off-diagonal) blocks lose their 'early-to-late' structure, whereas within-network (diagonal blocks) lag structure is preserved (Figure 5A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the TD matrix analysis shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Most cross-network blocks (excluding visual network pairs) appear disorganized during SWS.
source: Moreover, most cross-network blocks (excluding visual network pairs) appear disorganized during SWS.
evidence: This claim is supported by the TD matrix shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The dissociation between preserved within-network propagation and disorganized cross-network propagation suggests that neural communication during SWS is largely intact within functional networks (RSNs), but is disrupted across functional networks.
source: Speculatively, the dissociation between preserved within-network propagation and disorganized cross-network propagation suggests that neural communication during SWS, as measured by propagation of BOLD signals, is largely intact within functional networks (RSNs), but is disrupted across functional networks.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the present findings.

claim: These observations support theories postulating that reduced subjective awareness ('unconsciousness') during SWS results from loss of integration across networks.
source: These observations support theories postulating that reduced subjective awareness ('unconsciousness') during SWS results from loss of integration across networks (Mashour, 2005; Tononi, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mashour, 2005 and Tononi, 2004, and the present findings.

claim: Decreased subjective awareness during SWS theoretically results from loss of integration across networks, while within-network activity is generally preserved.
source: Accordingly, decreased subjective awareness during SWS theoretically results from loss of integration across networks, while within-network activity is generally preserved (Boly et al., 2012; Mashour, 2005; Tagliazucchi et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boly et al., 2012; Mashour, 2005; and Tagliazucchi et al., 2013a.

claim: During SWS, neural communication is maintained within functional modules, but altered across functional modules, resulting in 'network segregation'.
source: A corollary is that, during SWS, neural communication is maintained within functional modules, but altered across functional modules, resulting in 'network segregation' (Mashour, 2013; Tagliazucchi et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mashour, 2013 and Tagliazucchi et al., 2013a.

claim: During wake, the brain is capable of responding to the environment and functional systems reciprocally communicate to sustain conscious content.
source: During wake, the brain is capable of responding to the environment and functional systems reciprocally communicate to sustain conscious content (Alkire et al., 2008; McCormick et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alkire et al., 2008 and McCormick et al., 2015.

claim: Ascending BOLD signal propagation from thalamus to cortex is found during wake.
source: Accordingly, we find ascending BOLD signal propagation from thalamus to cortex (Figure 3A), as well as well-ordered propagation of activity between resting state networks (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Well-ordered propagation of activity between resting state networks is found during wake.
source: Accordingly, we find ascending BOLD signal propagation from thalamus to cortex (Figure 3A), as well as well-ordered propagation of activity between resting state networks (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Off-line brain activity during SWS theoretically serves mechanisms concerned with synaptic homeostasis and memory consolidation.
source: In SWS, off-line brain activity theoretically serves mechanisms concerned with synaptic homeostasis and memory consolidation (McClelland et al., 1995; McCormick et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McClelland et al., 1995 and McCormick et al., 2015.

claim: Features of the off-line state (SWS) include reduced responses to environmental stimuli, altered inter-network communication, but relatively intact intra-network communication.
source: Features of the off-line state (SWS) include reduced responses to environmental stimuli, altered inter-network communication, but relatively intact intra-network communication (McClelland et al., 1995; McNaughton et al. 2003; Tagliazucchi et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McClelland et al., 1995; McNaughton et al. 2003; and Tagliazucchi et al., 2013a.

claim: Reversal of thalamo-cortical propagation is observed during SWS.
source: Accordingly, we observe reversal of thalamo-cortical propagation (Figure 3A), altered cross-RSN propagation (Figure 5B-C), and intact within-RSN propagation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Altered cross-RSN propagation is observed during SWS.
source: Accordingly, we observe reversal of thalamo-cortical propagation (Figure 3A), altered cross-RSN propagation (Figure 5B-C), and intact within-RSN propagation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: Intact within-RSN propagation is observed during SWS.
source: Accordingly, we observe reversal of thalamo-cortical propagation (Figure 3A), altered cross-RSN propagation (Figure 5B-C), and intact within-RSN propagation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 63 non-sleep-deprived subjects were scanned in the evening.
source: 63 non-sleep-deprived subjects were scanned in the evening (starting at ∼8:00 PM).
evidence: This is a description of the study methodology.

claim: 39 subjects contributed to the present analyses.
source: These criteria yielded 39 subjects contributing to the present analyses.
evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claim: The study included 70 epochs of wakefulness, 47 epochs of N2 sleep, and 38 epochs of N3 sleep (SWS).
source: Included are 70 epochs of wakefulness, 47 epochs of N2 sleep, and 38 epochs of N3 sleep (SWS).
evidence: This is a description of the data included in the analysis.

claim: fMRI was acquired using a 3 T scanner with specific acquisition parameters.
source: fMRI was acquired using a 3 T scanner (Siemens Trio) with optimized polysomnographic settings (1,505 volumes of T2*-weighted echo planar images, repetition time/echo time = 2,080 ms/30 ms, matrix = 64 × 64, voxel size = 3 × 3 × 2 mm3, distance factor = 50%; field of view = 192 mm2).
evidence: This is a description of the data acquisition methodology.

claim: 30 EEG channels were simultaneously recorded using a modified cap with FCz as reference.
source: 30 EEG channels were simultaneously recorded using a modified cap (EASYCAP) with FCz as reference (sampling rate = 5 kHz, low pass filter = 250 Hz, high pass filter = 0.016 Hz).
evidence: This is a description of the EEG recording methodology.

claim: MRI and pulse artifact correction were performed based on the average artifact subtraction method.
source: MRI and pulse artifact correction were performed based on the average artifact subtraction method (Allen et al., 1998) as implemented in Vision Analyzer2 (Brain Products) followed by ICA-based rejection of residual artifact components (CBC parameters; Vision Analyzer).
evidence: This is a description of the data preprocessing methodology.

claim: EEG sleep staging was done by an expert according to the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) criteria.
source: EEG sleep staging was done by an expert according to the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) criteria (Soeffing et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a description of the sleep staging methodology.
